headline: New Haven Breakwall Porgies Run Deep, Charles Island Bass Go Nocturnal
subhead: Structure fishing is carrying the week while the stripers slide into the dark — here's where the rockpiles are paying off.
body_markdown:
Six-thirty Tuesday morning, outside the New Haven breakwall, and my rod tip is doing that little tap-tap-tap that means porgies are stacked under the boat and hungry. Two guys anchored off my stern were snapping their fingers trying to figure out why I had four fish in the bucket before they'd gotten bit once. Simple answer: I dropped a size 4 hook with a sliver of squid right on the up-current edge of the rockpile, not the flat sand ten feet off it. That's the whole game out here right now — inches matter, and the fish are exactly where the structure breaks the current, not where it's convenient to anchor.

The porgy bite on the New Haven Harbor breakwalls has been steady and honest all week, not spectacular, but you can count on it. High-hook boats are running double bottom rigs with size 4 to 6 hooks, squid strips or sandworm, working the outside face of the wall in 12 to 18 feet on the last two hours of the incoming and the first hour of the outgoing. That current-edge window is when the bait gets stirred up and the porgies commit. Once the tide goes fully slack, they scatter and sulk, so if you're only getting one shot this week, fish the change, not the middle of the tide.

Sea bass are riding shotgun with the porgies on the same structure, and some of them are quality — I had a 17-incher come off the Charles Island rockpile Thursday that made my Ugly Stik bend like a bow. The black sea bass are holding tight to the rougher stuff, the boulder fields and the mussel-crusted rubble on the northeast corner of Charles Island and out around Falkner Island, where the bottom drops from 10 feet down to 25 in a hurry. Green crab or squid on a knocker rig, dropped right into the crevices, has been the ticket. Don't be afraid to lose a few rigs — if you're not getting hung up occasionally you're probably not close enough to the rock.

Blackfish are a slower story right now. Tautog like it a little cooler than what we're running, and with Kings Point reading better than 71 and the whole western Sound carrying that same warmth, the tog have gone quiet during daylight compared to spring. I've had a couple decent fish, 4 and 6 pounds, off Stratford Shoal on green crab fished tight to the rockpile base on a moving tide, but it's been one or two fish for an hour of work rather than a fill-the-cooler morning. I'd call blackfish a bonus right now, not a plan.

Stripers are the one that's testing patience. The water's pushed into the low-to-mid 70s through the western and central Sound, and the bass have done what warm-water bass do — they've gone deep and gone nocturnal. I fished the Charles Island sandbar on the last of the outgoing at first light Sunday and got exactly nothing, then talked to a guy at the ramp who'd worked that same bar at 5 a.m. with a big walk-the-dog plug and put two schoolies and a 28-incher in the boat before the sun cleared the trees. That's the pattern now — dawn patrol and after-dark, working the drop where the sandbar falls into deeper water on the outgoing tide, live eels or bunker chunks if you can get them, swimming plugs if you're working the surface in that gray light. Midday, forget it — those fish are sitting deep off Stratford Shoal and the drop-offs around Falkner, not up shallow where you can reach them easy.

Fluke have been the pleasant surprise. We flagged this shift coming — that back-bay fluke would push out toward inlet mouths and the harder structure as the shallow water warmed past comfortable — and that's exactly what's showing now around the Milford Gulf and the deeper flats off Charles Island. Keeper-sized fish, several in the 18 to 20-inch class, are coming on white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the channel edges in 20 to 28 feet on the outgoing tide. If you're marking bait on the finder anywhere near the Gulf's deeper cuts, slow your drift down and work it twice.

Bluefish have been mostly a harbor-mouth story — schoolies chopping bait pods near the New Haven breakwalls on bright afternoons, nothing like the blitz conditions farther down the coast, but if you throw a small metal like a half-ounce Kastmaster into a nervous patch of bait you'll get bit.

Looking ahead: the moon's sliding toward first quarter on the 21st, which should ease the current push a touch and make the rip zones fish a little slower and more deliberate — good news for porgy and sea bass guys working bottom rigs, since a hard-ripping tide makes it tough to stay pinned to the rock. If the calm weather holds, I'd spend my week mornings on the breakwalls and Falkner for porgy and sea bass, and save one dawn or dusk session for the Charles Island bar with a plug rod, because that's still where the bigger bass are going to show if they show at all. Blackfish and daytime striper guys, I'd wait for a real cool-down before betting the whole trip on it.
